name: Hosts File
os_min: Windows 2000 (path has remained stable through current Windows releases)
purpose: Plain-text, manually-maintained IP-to-hostname mapping table that the DNS Client consults before querying any DNS server; lets an administrator, or an attacker, override name resolution for specific domains without touching DNS infrastructure.
normal_baseline: Ships with only commented example lines and, on many systems, a single localhost mapping (127.0.0.1 localhost / ::1 localhost); no active third-party entries.
anomalies: Entries redirecting security-vendor, Windows Update, or telemetry domains to 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1 (defense/update crippling)
Entries redirecting a legitimate domain (bank, SSO/MFA provider) to an attacker-controlled IP for credential harvesting, or to localhost specifically to break MFA callback traffic
File modification timestamp falling outside any known admin change window, or the file made hidden/read-only to resist casual edits

Unexpected growth into a long list of redirect entries, which can indicate either malicious blocking/redirection or a legitimate ad-blocking hosts file — intent must be judged by the specific target domains
parsing_tools: diff against a known-good baseline hosts file
File-integrity monitoring or EDR alerting on writes to the etc\hosts path
anti_forensic_notes: A plain text file with no built-in audit trail of its own; NTFS timestamp metadata and any file-write telemetry (e.g. Sysmon Event ID 11) are the only artifacts of when it changed, and both can be altered by an attacker with sufficient privilege. Its contents are also preloaded into the volatile DNS client cache, so a redirect may still be visible in ipconfig /displaydns even after the hosts file itself has been reverted.
